summary:
Yozgat province has no trans-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern documented in the sources. That absence records an absence of evidence of divergence from Turkey's national position rather than local safety: the national rules set out below reach Yozgat unchanged.

Turkey has no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers, and the documented exposure points lie inside the country rather than at the frontier. The visitor-facing document risk is general: foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. That requirement intersects with identity checks on the street. In August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after 'General Information Gathering' background checks. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detainee's account captures the practical position: nothing was fined, but names and details were recorded, and officers were already applying a regime that had not been enacted.

Criminalisation by statute had not been enacted when Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025, but a leaked omnibus draft then before the government, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' with up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, behind mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns it would force treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

Hostility toward LGBTI+ people in Turkey has hardened into explicit state policy. Kaos GL's 2025 review, 'The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People', records 'Year of the Family' instructions issued to public institutions and, for the first time in years, the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation, with expression and artistic freedom restricted and events cancelled or banned. The review counts 313 liberty violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the previous total, alongside 299 detention decisions; 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the prior year; 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected; private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, including obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy; and 61 travel bans. Turkish Minute's coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings.

Trans visitors who are detained are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare. Some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent.

Policing asymmetry is documented at the level of individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. Comparable asymmetry recurs in custody: on 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara, and rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to detention practices affecting transgender prisoners. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Event attendance carries its own exposure. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Protection machinery is thin. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity. The European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. If medication is needed during a stay, hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.
tangentialFactors:
The legislative position remains unsettled. The 11th Judicial Package was a leaked draft when Human Rights Watch reported it on 29 October 2025, and the sources do not record whether it has since been enacted, amended or withdrawn. A visitor planning around the current law is therefore reading a regime that officials have signalled they intend to widen, and the same gap between announced and enacted rules appears at street level in the August 2025 Istanbul stops, where officers applied checks that had no statutory basis.

Turkey's trajectory can be measured against its own recent past rather than against other countries. Kaos GL's year-on-year figures show the direction clearly: liberty violations up about two and a half times, torture and ill-treatment violations from 51 to 89, private-life violations from 16 to 67. The 2025 closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation is described by the monitor as the first in years, which places the current period outside the range of ordinary enforcement.

The gender-identity-specific elements of the draft package are the part with no precedent in the inventory: raising the age for gender-affirming care to 25 conditioned on permanent infertility, and criminal liability for the clinicians who provide it. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the provision, and Human Rights Watch expects it to push care underground rather than suppress demand.

Violence statistics in the sources are monitor-derived and compiled by civil-society organisations rather than published by the Turkish authorities, so they should be read as documented minimums. The Kaos GL review and Turkish Minute's account of it agree on the three hate-motivated killings and on the disproportionate effect on trans people.
localsOnly:
Residents of Yozgat live under the same national framework as visitors, but with no exit from it. Travel bans were imposed 61 times in 2025 according to Kaos GL, a restriction that binds residents directly and has no equivalent for a visitor who can leave.

'Year of the Family' instructions were issued to public institutions across the country, which reaches public-sector employment, schooling and municipal services in Yozgat as elsewhere. The first closure in years of an LGBTI+ rights organisation and the cancellation or banning of events constrain the organisations a resident would otherwise rely on for support, legal referral and documentation.

Obstruction of hormone therapy appears among the private-life violations recorded for 2025. Because hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, residents as well as visitors must obtain it privately and pay for it themselves, which puts continuity of supply at risk under any tightening of the rules on gender-affirming care.

Detention conditions fall hardest on residents. Facilities are organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and LGBTI+ detainees face arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation, restricted healthcare, frequent transfers and complaints procedures that are ineffective and can provoke further violence. The death of the transgender prisoner Poyraz at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025, and the delayed arrival of medical staff and investigators, describes custody as residents would encounter it.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents any Yozgat-specific enforcement, incident, arrest or facility treatment involving a trans person. The province-level entry rests on the national framework reaching Yozgat, not on local reporting, and no local monitor is cited.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted is unresolved. The inventory records the leaked draft and the opposition to it as of 29 October 2025 and stops there.

The claim that the August 2025 Istanbul 'General Information Gathering' checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights is attributed to legal experts quoted by bianet; no court ruling on those specific stops is cited.

Counts of violations, detentions, torture complaints, travel bans and hate killings come from Kaos GL's 2025 monitoring review and from Turkish Minute's reporting of it. Official Turkish government statistics for the same categories are not in the inventory.

Details of Poyraz's death on 1 December 2025 are attributed to other trans prisoners, visiting lawyers, rights groups and an opposition MP. Whether an independent investigation was opened or any charges followed is not sourced.
